would be contradicted by the ledger it cites.

WHAT I THINK THE HONEST FINDING IS -- and I am separating what I MEASURED from
what I INFER, because your row has to stand up:

  MEASURED: CPU-seconds +9.0%, wall +2.2%, cpu_ratio 29.88 -> 31.88.
  INFERRED: your campaign ADDS CONTENT. Two new peoples (duergar,
  mountain-dwarf) on top of roughly fifteen is about +13% peoples, and this run
  is also the first to carry the-wanderers' sky. More entities per world is more
  work per world. A ~9% CPU increase against ~13% more peoples is at or below
  proportional, which is the shape of added content rather than of an
  algorithmic regression.

  I have NOT verified proportionality. I did not measure per-people cost, and I
  cannot separate your peoples from the wanderers' sky in this number. If you
  want the row to claim proportionality, that needs one more measurement; if
  you want it to claim only "content grew and CPU grew no faster", the numbers
  above already support it.

THE TEST IS EXPLICIT THAT ACKNOWLEDGING WITHOUT LOOKING IS THE FAILURE IT
REPLACED — the previous version accepted a registry row, which any single run
could satisfy for every future one. So a row that says "new peoples, expected"
with no decomposition is exactly what it is built to reject. The four rows above
yours pass because each one DECOMPOSED the ledger. Yours can too, and I have
just done most of it.

The alarm exists to catch O(n^2) entering as a yellow run long before it is an
obvious one. Yours is the first run in a while where CPU genuinely moved, which
is precisely when the question is worth asking rather than waved through.
